blocks.prompt: The Tallest Hat in the Kitchen
blocks.text: A chef is the boss of a kitchen. The word chef is French. It means chief, or head. So a chef is the head cook. Chefs wear a tall white hat called a toque. Long ago, the tallest hat in the room belonged to the person in charge. The hat also keeps hair out of the food. Before a chef cooks anything, the chef gets ready. Onions get chopped. Pans get set out. Cooks call this mise en place. It means everything in its place. When the orders come in, there is no time to look for the salt. It has to be right there already.

blocks.prompt: Yes, Chef
blocks.text: Walk into a busy restaurant kitchen and the first thing you notice is the noise. A cook calls out an order. Everyone answers, yes, chef. It sounds like a soldier answering a captain, and that is almost exactly what it is. A French chef named Georges Auguste Escoffier ran kitchens more than a hundred years ago. Before him, kitchens were chaos. Cooks argued, shouted, and got in each other's way. Escoffier had been a cook in the French army, so he built the kitchen like an army. He gave every cook one station and one job. One cook made sauces. One cooked fish. One made desserts. Nobody wandered. Nobody guessed. He called it the brigade. The hat came from the same idea. A chef's tall white hat is a toque. For a long time, the taller your hat, the higher your rank. The head chef wore the tallest one, so anyone glancing across a steaming kitchen knew instantly who was in charge. Some cooks still say the pleats in a toque stand for one hundred ways to cook an egg. Nobody has proved that. Chefs like the story anyway.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

Brigade: one cook, one station
The saucier makes sauces

blocks.prompt: Everything in Its Place
blocks.text: Ask a professional cook what the hardest part of the job is and you will rarely hear cooking. You will hear prep. A restaurant kitchen has a strange problem. Nobody orders anything for hours, and then, at seven in the evening, forty people order forty different things at once. Every plate has to be hot, correct, and finished within minutes. A cook who starts chopping an onion when the order arrives has already lost. So cooks solve the problem before it happens. They arrive hours early and build what the French call mise en place, which means putting in place. Onions diced. Herbs picked. Sauces simmered and strained. Stock reduced. Butter softened. Every container sits in the same spot on the same shelf, every single day, so a cook can reach for it without looking. By the time the first order prints, the cooking is almost the easy part. It is assembly. The system underneath all of this was designed by Georges Auguste Escoffier, a French chef who had served in the army. He split the kitchen into stations and gave each one a leader. The saucier made sauces. The poissonnier cooked fish. The patissier made desserts. The chef de cuisine, the head of the kitchen, stood at the pass and checked every plate before it left. It sounds rigid. It is. That is the point. Rigid systems are what let a kitchen absorb chaos on a Saturday night without falling apart.

notes: The Maillard reaction was described in 1912

blocks.prompt: Why Brown Food Tastes Better
blocks.text: Put a piece of raw meat next to a cooked one. Same meat, same animal. One smells like almost nothing. The other smells like dinner from across the house. Something happened in the pan, and it was not just heat. In 1912, a French chemist named Louis Camille Maillard was studying how amino acids react with sugars. He was not thinking about food at all. What he found is now named after him, and it is arguably the single most important process in cooking. When protein and sugar meet at high heat, roughly above 285 degrees Fahrenheit, they do not simply get hot. They rearrange. They fall apart and recombine into hundreds of brand new compounds that did not exist a minute earlier. Those compounds are the smell of toast, of seared steak, of roasted coffee, of the crust on bread. The browning you see is the visible edge of an enormous invisible chemical event. This is why chefs are so serious about a dry surface and a hot pan. Water boils at 212 degrees. As long as the surface of the meat is wet, the pan cannot climb high enough for the reaction to run. The meat steams instead, and gray steamed meat tastes like disappointment. Pat it dry, get the pan properly hot, leave it alone, and the reaction takes over. Chefs will also tell you, confidently, that searing seals in the juices. This is not true. It was proposed by a chemist named Justus von Liebig in the 1840s, repeated in cookbooks for a hundred and fifty years, and tested carefully in the twentieth century. Seared meat actually loses slightly more moisture, not less. The sear is worth doing anyway, just for a different reason than the one everybody gives. It is not a seal. It is flavor. That gap is worth noticing. A good cook can be completely right about what to do and completely wrong about why. The steak still works. But knowing the real reason is what lets you use the same idea somewhere new, on an onion, on a scallop, on the top of a pie.

6.title: The Tallest Hat in the Kitchen

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Careme, 1784 to 1833: cooking built like architecture
Escoffier, 1846 to 1935: the brigade system
Le Guide Culinaire, 1903, still opened by cooks
Restaurant first meant a restoring broth
Toque height once marked rank
Chef de cuisine: head of the kitchen

blocks.prompt: The Men Who Made Cooking a Profession
blocks.text: For most of human history, cooking was work you did because someone had to. It was not a career you announced with pride. Two Frenchmen changed that, and the kitchen you would walk into today still runs on their decisions. The first was Marie-Antoine Careme, born in Paris in 1784, one of a very large and very poor family. As a boy he was left at the city gates and told not to come back. He found work washing dishes in a cheap eating house, then apprenticed to a pastry maker, and taught himself to read in the print room of the national library, studying books of architecture. That last detail matters. Careme built his desserts like buildings: towering sugar temples, ruins, and bridges, drawn out on paper first and assembled to the inch. He cooked for Talleyrand, for the future king of England, and for the Russian tsar. He once wrote that there are five fine arts, painting, poetry, music, sculpture, and architecture, and that the principal branch of architecture is confectionery. He was joking. He was also not joking at all. The second was Georges Auguste Escoffier, born in 1846. Careme had made cooking glamorous. Escoffier made it work. He had cooked for the French army during the war of 1870, and he came out of it thinking about logistics rather than glory. Old kitchens were furnaces of shouting, drinking, and duplicated effort, where one dish might pass through the hands of four cooks who each did whatever they felt like. Escoffier tore that up. He divided the kitchen into stations, a brigade, each with a chief: sauces, fish, roasts, cold dishes, pastry. Each cook owned one narrow territory and answered to the chef de cuisine, the head of the kitchen. A single plate could now be built by five people in ninety seconds without a word wasted. He banned shouting in his kitchens. He banned drinking on shift. He asked his cooks to be clean, quiet, and on time, which sounds obvious now and was radical then. He also had a place to put the system. Working with the hotelier Cesar Ritz at the Savoy in London and later at the Ritz in Paris, Escoffier fed rooms full of people who could go anywhere and expected everything. His book, Le Guide Culinaire, published in 1903, wrote the whole method down. Cooks still open it. The stage had been set slightly earlier. The word restaurant comes from the French verb meaning to restore. In Paris in the 1760s, shops sold a rich, concentrated broth called a restaurant, sold as a cure for weak health. The shops eventually took the name of the soup. Then the Revolution broke up the great households, and their cooks, suddenly unemployed and highly skilled, had somewhere to go. Cooking left the palace and went public. Anyone with money, not just anyone with a title, could now taste it. What Careme and Escoffier really built was not a menu. It was an argument, made in brass pans and written schedules, that cooking deserved to be treated as serious work by serious people. The tall white hat is a leftover from that argument. It marked rank in a room where rank had suddenly started to mean something. It is worth asking what the argument cost. The brigade is efficient because it is hierarchical, and hierarchies are easy to abuse. For a century, the professional kitchen has been famous for brutal hours, low pay, and shouting that Escoffier himself tried to ban. The system that made cooks respected is the same system that has often ground them down. Both things came out of the same idea, and the industry is still arguing about whether it can keep one without the other.
